transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

It may well be worth fixing, but it depends which side of the drive system has failed. On a roughly nine-year-old Indesit, a belt fault or worn motor brushes can be a sensible repair; a failed motor, control board or worn drum bearings can be harder to justify against replacement. The more likely causes are:
1. A slipped or snapped drive belt, if it is a belt-driven version — especially if you can hear the motor running but the drum stays still.
2. Worn carbon brushes or another motor-drive fault — more likely if there is no attempt from the motor to turn the drum.
3. A jammed drum or bearing issue — more likely if it feels stiff, rough or grinds when turned by hand. 1. Switch off at the socket and unplug it. With the drum empty, turn it by hand. It should rotate smoothly with only normal resistance. If it is stiff, catches, grinds or has obvious up-and-down looseness, stop using it; that points towards a mechanical repair rather than a simple belt/brush job.
2. Put it back together normally, select a short wash or spin programme, and listen without removing any panels. Can you hear a hum or motor whirr while the drum remains still? A motor sound with a freely turning drum makes a belt fault more likely; no motor sound makes brushes, motor control or wiring more likely. If the drum is free and there is a motor noise, an engineer can usually confirm the belt quickly. If it is mechanically rough or loose, or there is burning smell, smoke or heavy sparking, leave it unplugged and arrange an engineer rather than keep testing it.

I unplugged it and turned the drum by hand. It turns freely and quietly, with no scraping or rumble. With it running on a short programme I can hear clicking, which sounds like relays, but no motor noise at all. I did notice a faint hot electrical smell a few weeks ago, though not since. Where do we go from here?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. The next step is a qualified appliance engineer; it must not be used again until it has been checked. The freely turning, quiet drum makes seized bearings or an obstruction unlikely. As it fills and drains, then only clicks with no motor sound, the fault is most likely in the motor-drive side: worn carbon brushes if it has a brushed motor, a burned/loose motor connection, the motor itself, or the motor-control module. The earlier hot electrical smell makes a brush or connection fault more plausible. A broken belt is less likely because normally you would still hear the motor running. It can still be worth repairing at nine years old if it proves to be brushes, a belt, or a repairable connection. A failed motor or control board is the point at which it becomes sensible to ask for a fixed diagnostic/repair quote and compare it with replacement. Ask the engineer to inspect the motor brushes where applicable, motor wiring/connectors, belt and motor-control board for heat damage before condemning a major part. The full model number from the rating label around the door opening or on the back will help them identify the correct drive arrangement.

candidates: Drive belt fault (if this is a belt-driven version) (medium)
Worn motor carbon brushes or another motor-drive fault (medium)
